content:
Hi everyone! :wave:

I have been maintaining and evolving Archon, a harness for autoformalization automation, a project I actively maintain and will continue to support.
However, the next generation of LLMs seem to be becoming increasingly autonomous in agentic tasks, as the recent preview of Fable 5 confirmed. This raises the question of how to build harnesses around these future agents. While Archon worked well with Fable 5, I noticed that Fable 5 took more liberties than Opus 4.8: its sessions were much longer, and it sometimes even stopped following some prompts.

Therefore, I have started developing a successor to Archon (perhaps better viewed as an alternative than a replacement, Archon remains active) optimized specifically for long-horizon agents, currently (temporarily ?) named Archon Horizon. While I already have a working initial version, since this project is starting fresh and isn't released yet, its structure is still very flexible, I'd like to gather community suggestions first and understand how you would ideally use such a system. Many people in our community currently autoformalize with a minimal harness (or none at all), which is lightweight and intuitive. However, the main strength of a dedicated harness is scalability, consistency and maintainability on massive projects.

I will summarize my main ideas for this new project here:

  • Workspaces instead of single projects: While a workspace can contain just one project if you want, it can also contain N related (or not) projects inside the same workspace and easily manage the interplay between them. For instance, if project C requires infrastructure created in project B, you can work on their union or extract a shared project BC and import it in project B and project C, etc.
  • Beyond mathlib dependencies: A workspace can specify external projects (not only mathlib) in its dependencies. Since independent formalization repos can grow very large now that autoformalization is evolving, it should rely on a robust search engine inside the workspace, whether for retrieving information from the external projects or even the workspace's projects.
  • A freer dual-agent balance: The proof execution harness is much lighter than Archon's, giving the agent more freedom (As I said, I suspect Fable 5 and others of its kind of being very free), while a secondary high-level agent remains more constrained to ensure the project doesn't diverge and stays clean, also taking care of making human-readable artifacts.
  • Human-directed collaboration: While the broader trend is to push humans out of the loop, I want to do the opposite. The system can run fully autonomously, but the human should remain the main controller with a clear understanding of what is going on, and a strong influence. If your workspace has a GitHub repository, you can easily route issues/PRs directly to Archon Horizon. Moreover, every interaction between agents / agent-human / parallel runs, would all communicate in a similar way, sending issues that the others read when they open it, and can close, organise by priority, etc.
  • Long-term projects scalability: My aim is a system capable of coordinating formalizations much larger than the Jacobian Challenge without hitting context window degradation. This is the other reason why I'd prefer working in workspaces than projects. I'd like project management to be smooth, for instance a project like AG Jacobian is complete, we may want to extend the workspace to more Algebraic Geometry.

I am very interested in your thoughts: What are your needs, ideas, and suggestions? In what kinds of formalization projects would you want to use a system like this, and what are your expectations for future agent tooling?
I think some of the features you mentioned have already been implemented in Lumina Fuse. I've been trying it out, and it's been working really well for me. Might be worth taking a look!

Jinzheng Li said :

I think some of the features you mentioned have already been implemented in Lumina Fuse. I've been trying it out, and it's been working really well for me. Might be worth taking a look!

Since Archon is an open-source, user-driven project, I don't think they are entirely comparable even if they serve a similar purpose. The main appeal of Archon is that it is shaped by the community, users frequently propose features through PRs that get directly integrated. Furthermore, our project works without requiring separate API keys, instead utilizing the user's existing Claude or Codex accounts, which is much more cheaper. Which specific features were you referring to?

The current version of Archon already shares a similar workflow with Numina. However, the successor project I am talking about focuses on autoformalization optimized specifically for upcoming models like Fable 5. Their reasoning capabilities are entirely different, which seems to require a separate framework from Archon, and I haven't seen anything like that being built anywhere else yet, so I am curious if Numina Fuse already integrates it.

Yes, I just meant that Numina Fuse is a good reference to keep in mind for this new project.

As for preparing for Fable 5, my experience has been that applying a new model almost always requires some redesign of the harness. Every model has its own unique strengths and weaknesses, so we really need tailored prompts and harness to unlock their full potential. This is exactly where I think a self-evolving harness could play a major role.

Jinzheng Li said :

Yes, I just meant that Numina Fuse is a good reference to keep in mind for this new project.

As for preparing for Fable 5, my experience has been that applying a new model almost always requires some redesign of the harness. Every model has its own unique strengths and weaknesses, so we really need tailored prompts and harness to unlock their full potential. This is exactly where I think a self-evolving harness could play a major role.

I considered self-evolving harness, for instance letting some agent modify the prompts, or maybe adding some blocs of the code that are modular and can be modified safely. Nevertheless, I am worried about letting such freedom. Indeed, when I wrote code for Archon, I used several agents like Codex, Antigravity, CC, but I always need to modify a lot by hand, all the more for the prompts, the agents tend to overfit the prompts to the situation, or make the prompts worsen their false hypotheses, etc. I fear the behaviour of such systems might diverge quickly from the expectations. Do you have a specific idea on implementing such self-evolving harness, or specific projects which use it ?

My current solution is to make Archon Horizon a 2-agents-system, a first one which is constrained, with specific instructions, a second one which is much freer, able to choose how they want to handle the situation. There is not really self-evolution, but I expect the free agent to create the tools they want, to create subagents or skills or whatever when they need, to refactor the workspace as they want, while the constrained agent would verify there is no divergence and so some reporting task for human/dashboard, it can also send warnings to the other agents, and manage the global memory, which is somewhat similar to modifying the prompts.

In my view, for a large-scale formalization project, one of the key issues is how to build and maintain many Mathlib-style structures / typeclasses. At the moment, although LLM-as-a-judge approaches, or some operator-tree / syntax-tree-based methods, can help check whether natural-language statements and formalized Lean statements are aligned to some extent, the final confirmation still has to be done by humans.

Because of this, I have always felt that mathematicians need a clearly auditable scope and an auditable interface when working with this kind of agent-based workflow.

I wonder if you have heard of the Trellis project（https://github.com/wpegden/trellis）. Recently, I ran more than 400 rounds of Trellis on a mathematical paper formalization project, consuming 93% of my weekly budget of $200 GPT Auth. However, it still was not able to fully formalize the whole paper. I am currently analyzing its codebase as well, hoping to get more insight from it.

One design question I wanted to ask is whether you have considered storing each mathematical object separately as a pair consisting of a TeX / natural-language representation and a Lean representation, instead of storing everything only in the traditional form of whole Lean files. Or, at least, whether there could be some mechanism that allows control and auditing at the level of individual mathematical-object nodes.

Of course, I am not saying that the DAG structure itself is new. Similar dependency-graph ideas have already appeared in blueprint-style workflows and in systems such as Trellis. What I am more interested in is how to build an auditing and evaluation layer on top of such a graph, especially for AI-generated formalization projects.

In my opinion, the existing blueprint mechanism is not sufficient for this purpose, because it usually assumes that the nodes are reliable. In an AI-generated setting, however, the nodes themselves may be unreliable: a node may compile, but still fail to faithfully capture the intended informal mathematics. Therefore, the nodes themselves need to become auditable objects.

In order to stay synchronized with very large, information-dense codebases, and also to keep the codebase synchronized with the mathematician’s understanding, I would like to develop an annotation and evaluation method for auditing formalized codebases produced by different agent systems. More concretely, the idea is to reduce or project a codebase into a DAG-like format: each node would contain a pairing between an informal mathematical statement and a formal Lean object, and each node would be scored along several dimensions. This would allow us to evaluate the actual completion level of a formalization project relative to the original paper or mathematical problem.

I expect the evaluation dimensions to include consistency, coverage, sorry-freeness, and so on. This also requires handling dependency relations between nodes. The audit scope could support two different modes:

  1. Checking whether all important mathematical nodes in the whole paper have been correctly formalized;

  2. Checking only one main theorem or conclusion in the paper, together with all the formalized objects it directly or indirectly depends on.

The second mode is essentially an “Audit Cone” structure. I think it would be useful for the system to support both modes.

Another issue is: for structures, definitions inheriting from structures, and various fields in a formalized codebase, which parts actually need to be audited? This probably also requires a rule-based filtering mechanism, so that mathematicians can focus their attention only on the parts where the alignment between informal mathematics and formal Lean code genuinely needs to be checked.

In fact, I have already started working in this direction, and I expect to have a demo in about one or two weeks. I am not sure whether this could potentially interact or integrate with Archon Horizon in some way, but I would be very happy to discuss this possibility further.

Thank you for the complete answer. I think it is going in the same direction as my current ideas. For the DAG structure of the project, I already have somehow integrated it by adding tools to interact with the dag structure and skills for the agents to do it. But it is currently minimal, and mostly just parsing of the Lean/blueprint files that agents write into. I also thought about making it the other way around, meaning that agents may only add / remove nodes from a dag structure, this would be optimal in an engineering pov. I am however wondering whether agents would benefit from it, since they are not trained to work with dag structures directly, but this may also give a constraint that the global project would benefit from though.
I will do some testing on this.

@Axel Delaval I've had great success on formalizing a project in differential geometry using archon. Currently using a forked version of 0.3.1 inside a docker image. With a human in the loop (as well as archon discuss ) it's an incredible harness in my opinion.
I would love to contribute some additions I've made, but I have gotten a bit lost w.r.t what version to use. I see there's a new 0.3.3, but I have also used your personal fork. Moreover, I'm curious about Archon Horizon which seems to be a superset of archon but with no open source repo. Would you be able to suggest what version to use and contribute towards?

Thank you for your feedback on Archon. If you believe that your fork can be adapted and PR-ed to Archon, don't hesitate, even if draftly, I'll try to make them adapt to the current code.

Let me explain the versions :

  • Archon is currently 0.3.3 (mostly patches of some bugs, and some small functionalities have been added, like the possibility to add a peers.yaml file in a project to make other Archon projects readable from it). If you are satisfied with your 0.3.1 fork, it is not so important to update.
  • Archon Horizon is more like a brother of Archon than a superset, Archon may be a better choice in some cases:
    - For powerful models like opus 5, gpt-5-sol, Fable 5, with ultra reasoning, Archon Horizon is a better choice. This is because these models are themselves harness, now codex/cc dispatch workflows and subagents natively, so Archon Horizon is made a very lightweight harness to take advantage of this.
    - For smaller models like deepseek, kimi, sonnet, gpt-5.5, maybe opus with standard reasoning, Archon is a better choice. Since these models might easily be overloaded by the context, they work better if they are divided in tasks "plan -> prove -> review".
    - For smaller projects, Archon is maybe a better choice
    - For big projects (e.g. formalizing several related textbooks in parallel), Archon Horizon is a more natural choice, since it natively works inside a workspace

We intend to make Archon Horizon public soon (maybe within 1/2 weeks), so that we can still change the code heavily without impacting users.

Thank you for this helpful overview. I'll stay on my fork for the remainder of this project but will probably give Archon Horizon a try on the next one. I understand what you mean with the more powerful models not being ideal for Archon. Sometimes I have fable/sol "out of the loop" advising the archon loop for this reason. I should also mention that I'm using Archon to do new mathematics, and not just formalize existing work. This is also why I often need to advice the loop from the outside.
